title: Button Battery Ingestion: Treat as Time-Critical Even Before Symptoms
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Suspected button-battery ingestion is a time-critical emergency because an esophageal battery can cause severe injury rapidly and the child may initially look well. Do not induce vomiting and do not delay emergency imaging/evaluation while waiting for symptoms.
recognize: Unexplained drooling, dysphagia, cough, wheeze, vomiting, chest discomfort, food refusal, choking, or a missing battery are concerning.
priorities: Activate poison/battery-ingestion guidance and emergency evaluation immediately.
assessMonitor: Airway, swallowing, drooling, respiratory status, pain, vomiting, GI bleeding, and time/type of possible ingestion.
interventions: Keep the child on the emergency pathway and follow poison-center/ED instructions; do not give routine food or fluids outside the specific battery protocol.
medicationSafety: Honey/sucralfate mitigation is age/time/situation specific and must never delay emergency removal of an esophageal battery.
teaching: Store button batteries locked away and secure battery compartments.
delegationScope: Emergency recognition and immediate escalation are appropriate; battery-location/removal decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Waiting for pain or fever because the child seems asymptomatic.
oneLinePearl: A swallowed button battery can injure before symptoms appear—do not wait.
sourceBasis: National Capital Poison Center button-battery guideline

title: Hydrocarbon Ingestion: Aspiration Risk Matters More Than Induced Vomiting
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Gasoline, kerosene, lighter fluid, furniture polish, and similar hydrocarbons can cause chemical pneumonitis if aspirated. Do not induce vomiting; respiratory symptoms drive urgency.
recognize: Coughing, choking, wheeze, tachypnea, hypoxemia, vomiting, or altered mental status after exposure are concerning.
priorities: Assess airway/breathing, contact poison-control/emergency resources, and escalate respiratory symptoms promptly.
assessMonitor: Respiratory rate/work, SpO2, cough, mental status, vomiting, and exposure substance/amount/time.
interventions: Remove contaminated clothing/skin exposure as appropriate and follow poison-center instructions.
medicationSafety: Activated charcoal and gastric emptying are not routine for aspiration-prone hydrocarbons and require toxicology direction.
teaching: Store fuels and solvents in original locked containers, never drink bottles.
delegationScope: Exposure history and monitoring may be shared; toxicology treatment decisions are provider/poison-center led.
examTrap: Inducing vomiting to remove the hydrocarbon from the stomach.
oneLinePearl: With hydrocarbons, getting it into the lungs can be worse than leaving it in the stomach.

title: Pediatric Iron Overdose: GI Symptoms Can Precede Severe Toxicity
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Iron-containing vitamins can cause dangerous pediatric poisoning. Vomiting, abdominal pain, bloody GI symptoms, lethargy, or suspected significant ingestion requires immediate poison-control/emergency evaluation.
recognize: A child may improve transiently before later systemic toxicity, so symptom improvement does not automatically end risk.
priorities: Identify product/strength if possible, assess ABCs, and contact poison-control/emergency services promptly.
assessMonitor: Mental status, GI symptoms, hemodynamics, glucose, acid-base status, and serum iron/liver studies as ordered.
interventions: Support IV fluids and antidotal/critical care directed by toxicology/provider.
medicationSafety: Do not calculate home treatment from pill counts alone; product elemental-iron content matters.
teaching: Keep prenatal vitamins and iron supplements locked away from children.
delegationScope: Immediate recognition/escalation is appropriate; chelation decisions are toxicology/provider led.
examTrap: Reassuring the family because vomiting stopped after several hours.
oneLinePearl: Iron overdose can look better before it gets worse.
sourceBasis: U.S. Poison Control pediatric iron-overdose principles

title: Acetaminophen Overdose: Early Wellness Does Not Rule Out Liver Injury
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: A child or adolescent with suspected acetaminophen overdose may initially have few symptoms. Prompt timing/history, serum testing, and toxicology-guided antidote decisions are essential.
recognize: Repeated supratherapeutic dosing, combination cold/analgesic products, self-harm ingestion, nausea, vomiting, or RUQ discomfort are cues.
priorities: Clarify product, dose/time if known, assess self-harm intent when relevant, and obtain urgent toxicology/ED evaluation.
assessMonitor: Mental status, GI symptoms, serum acetaminophen level, liver tests, INR, renal function, and glucose as ordered.
interventions: Administer N-acetylcysteine when ordered according to toxicology protocol.
medicationSafety: Do not use the single-acute-ingestion nomogram for repeated supratherapeutic exposure unless the clinician confirms applicability.
teaching: Check combination-product labels to avoid unintentional duplicate acetaminophen dosing.
delegationScope: Medication reconciliation and symptom monitoring are appropriate; antidote decisions are provider/toxicology led.
examTrap: Ruling out serious overdose because the patient looks well in the first hours.
oneLinePearl: Acetaminophen toxicity can be silent before the liver declares itself.

title: Salicylate Toxicity: Tachypnea, Vomiting, Tinnitus, or Confusion Need Urgent Evaluation
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Salicylate toxicity can produce tachypnea, vomiting, tinnitus, diaphoresis, fever, acid-base abnormalities, and altered mental status. Clinical deterioration matters even if a single serum level seems modest.
recognize: Repeated dosing and oil-of-wintergreen products can create major exposure.
priorities: Assess breathing/mental status, identify product/time, and obtain urgent poison-control/ED evaluation.
assessMonitor: Respiratory status, temperature, glucose, electrolytes, acid-base status, serial salicylate levels, and renal function as ordered.
interventions: Support fluids, glucose, alkalinization, and dialysis preparation only under toxicology/provider direction.
medicationSafety: Avoid sedating or intubating without expert planning when severe salicylate poisoning is suspected because ventilation changes can worsen acidemia.
teaching: Store aspirin and concentrated salicylate-containing products securely.
delegationScope: Focused monitoring is appropriate; toxicology and airway strategy are provider-led.
examTrap: Treating tachypnea only as anxiety and suppressing it without evaluating poisoning.
oneLinePearl: In salicylate toxicity, fast breathing may be protective—not just a symptom to stop.

title: Caustic Ingestion: Do Not Neutralize or Induce Vomiting
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Strong acid or alkali ingestion can burn the mouth, esophagus, and stomach. Do not induce vomiting or attempt home neutralization; drooling, stridor, dysphagia, chest/abdominal pain, or respiratory distress requires emergency care.
recognize: Oral burns may be absent despite deeper injury.
priorities: Assess airway first, identify the product, and activate poison-control/emergency evaluation.
assessMonitor: Voice, drooling, swallowing, respiratory status, pain, vomiting, abdominal findings, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Keep NPO unless directed otherwise and prepare for airway/endoscopic evaluation as ordered.
medicationSafety: Neutralizing one chemical with another can worsen injury and is not a home nursing intervention.
teaching: Store cleaners/chemicals locked in original containers.
delegationScope: Emergency recognition is immediate; airway/endoscopic decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Giving an acid after alkali ingestion to neutralize the chemical.
oneLinePearl: Caustic ingestion: protect the airway and do not create a second chemical reaction.

title: Pediatric Opioid Exposure: Somnolence Plus Slow Breathing Is an Emergency
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
bottomLine: Unexpected sleepiness, pinpoint pupils, slowed or ineffective breathing, cyanosis, or poor responsiveness after possible opioid exposure requires immediate ventilation support and naloxone/emergency response according to protocol.
recognize: Patches, pills, liquids, illicit fentanyl, and caregiver medications are potential sources.
priorities: Support airway/breathing, administer naloxone if authorized/available, and activate EMS.
assessMonitor: Respiratory rate/effort, SpO2, mental status, pupils, glucose as indicated, and response/recurrence after naloxone.
interventions: Provide rescue breathing/oxygen and repeat naloxone only per emergency protocol while awaiting definitive care.
medicationSafety: Naloxone may wear off before the opioid, so apparent recovery does not eliminate monitoring need.
teaching: Lock opioids and dispose of unused medication safely; keep naloxone where recommended.
delegationScope: Emergency BLS/naloxone use depends on training/protocol; ongoing toxicology management is provider-led.
examTrap: Letting the child sleep after naloxone because breathing briefly improved.
oneLinePearl: Naloxone can reverse the moment, not necessarily the whole exposure.

title: Pediatric Cannabis Edible Exposure: Altered Mental Status Can Be Significant
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Young children can develop marked somnolence, ataxia, vomiting, tachycardia, or respiratory compromise after edible cannabis exposure. A caregiver's assumption that it is harmless does not replace assessment.
recognize: Unexplained sleepiness or imbalance after access to gummies, baked products, concentrates, or household cannabis is a clue.
priorities: Assess ABCs/mental status, verify glucose when indicated, contact poison-control/emergency services, and consider alternative causes of altered mental status.
assessMonitor: Respiratory status, arousability, gait if safe, vomiting, vital signs, and co-ingestant possibility.
interventions: Provide supportive observation and airway protection as needed.
medicationSafety: Do not give unapproved stimulants or home remedies to wake the child.
teaching: Store edibles locked and clearly separated from ordinary food/candy.
delegationScope: Observation is appropriate; diagnosis and disposition are provider/poison-center led.
examTrap: Assuming a sleepy child only needs to nap after known edible ingestion.
oneLinePearl: Edibles can cause profound pediatric CNS effects even when adults expect mild intoxication.
sourceBasis: U.S. Poison Control pediatric cannabis principles

title: Lead Exposure: Most Children Look Well—Risk History Drives Testing
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Most children with lead exposure have no obvious immediate symptoms. Exposure history and blood lead testing—not appearance alone—identify risk.
recognize: Older housing/renovation dust, contaminated soil/water/products, imported remedies/spices, occupational take-home exposure, and pica increase risk.
priorities: Identify exposure risk and ensure appropriate blood testing/follow-up.
assessMonitor: Development, behavior, growth, nutrition/iron status, exposure sources, and blood lead results as ordered.
interventions: Reinforce environmental source removal, nutrition guidance, public-health follow-up, and chelation only when prescribed.
medicationSafety: Chelation is not a substitute for removing the exposure source and is used only under specific clinical criteria.
redFlags: Severe abdominal symptoms in a high-exposure context
teaching: No visible symptoms does not mean lead exposure is harmless; testing is key.
delegationScope: Risk-screening reinforcement is appropriate; public-health and treatment decisions follow protocol/provider direction.
examTrap: Skipping testing because the child has normal growth and behavior today.
oneLinePearl: Lead poisoning is often silent—test risk, not just symptoms.
sourceBasis: CDC Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention guidance updated 2026

title: Pediatric Carbon Monoxide Exposure: Multiple Sick Household Members Is a Clue
bottomLine: Headache, dizziness, weakness, vomiting, confusion, syncope, or multiple household members with similar flu-like illness can indicate carbon monoxide poisoning. Remove from exposure and obtain emergency evaluation; routine pulse oximetry can appear deceptively normal.
recognize: Fuel-burning heaters, generators, fires, and enclosed-engine exposure are common sources.
priorities: Move to fresh air if safe, activate EMS/fire resources, and support high-concentration oxygen per emergency protocol.
assessMonitor: Mental status, respiratory/cardiovascular status, exposure duration/source, co-oximetry and cardiac testing as ordered.
interventions: Provide oxygen and prepare for hyperbaric consultation when indicated by the treating team.
medicationSafety: A normal standard SpO2 does not rule out CO poisoning.
teaching: Use functioning CO alarms and never run generators or combustion devices in enclosed/attached spaces.
delegationScope: Emergency support is immediate; hyperbaric/disposition decisions are provider-led.
examTrap: Ruling out CO poisoning because pulse oximetry reads 99%.
oneLinePearl: CO can hide behind a normal pulse-ox number.
sourceBasis: CDC Carbon Monoxide Poisoning Basics updated 2026
